learningObjective: Explain why a CPU-based timer around a CUDA kernel launch loop under-reports GPU execution time and how to obtain a correct measurement.

canonicalClaims.claim: CUDA kernel launches are asynchronous with respect to the CPU; a CPU-side timer around a launch loop without synchronization measures dispatch cost, not GPU execution time. Wrapping the region with `torch.cuda.synchronize()` (or equivalent stream sync) before starting and after stopping the timer yields the correct wall time.
conditions: The launch is on the default stream (or any stream that is drained by the chosen synchronization primitive).
The measured region contains enough GPU work that the sync cost is negligible.
nonImplications: Does not imply CPU timers are always inferior; they are fine for aggregate throughput measurements when framed by synchronization.
Does not imply that `torch.cuda.Event.elapsed_time` is required; it is preferable for individual-kernel timing but not for a whole loop.

misconceptions.claim: `torch.cuda.synchronize()` returns before all kernels finish and cannot be relied on for timing.
misconceptions.whyWrong: `torch.cuda.synchronize()` blocks the host until all kernels on the current device's default stream have completed.

misconceptions.claim: A 4096-square FP32 matmul actually executes in ~ 8 µs on modern GPUs; the CPU-timer number is correct.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Even at A100 FP32 peak (19.5 TFLOP/s), 4096³·2 ≈ 137 GFLOP takes ~ 7 ms; 8 µs is impossible.

misconceptions.claim: The 400× discrepancy between the two attempts is explained by CUDA JIT warmup effects.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Warmup effects exist (kernel loading, cuBLAS handle init) but are one-time costs, not per-iteration; they do not explain a per-iter 400× gap.

misconceptions.claim: Using `time.perf_counter()` around CUDA launches is fundamentally invalid; only CUDA Events can measure GPU work.
misconceptions.whyWrong: CPU timers with proper synchronization measure GPU wall time correctly; CUDA Events are preferable for microsecond-scale per-kernel measurement.

implementationFacts: CUDA launch returns after the driver enqueues the kernel, before the GPU finishes
`torch.cuda.synchronize()` blocks host until all preceding work on the current device completes
performanceScenarios: Benchmarking harness pattern: (1) warm up N iterations, (2) synchronize, (3) start CPU timer, (4) launch M iterations, (5) synchronize, (6) stop CPU timer, (7) divide by M.
